A.explanation: True value is always less than meter reading and the gap $reading - true$ grows with voltage, showing a varying systematic over-read.

B.explanation: The line is $true \approx reading$, which would mean almost no systematic error, not a meter that reads high.

C.explanation: For most of the range true value is greater than meter reading, which means under-reading, opposite to the description.

D.explanation: True value is greater than meter reading and there is a positive intercept near $0.2 \text{ V}$, which means under-reading with a zero error.

hints: Notice the axes: vertical is true value in $\text{V}$ and horizontal is meter reading in $\text{V}$, so over-reading means each point must lie below the line $true = reading$.
Think what varying systematic error means for the gap $reading - true$: a constant zero error would shift the line, while a gap that grows with voltage changes the slope or curvature.
Compare each graph at e.g. meter reading $= 2 \text{ V}$ and $4 \text{ V}$: check whether true is smaller, and whether the difference gets larger at higher voltage.
walkthrough: Identify the calibration axes: $y$ = true value / $\text{V}$, $x$ = meter reading / $\text{V}$. A perfect meter would give $y = x$.
Over-reading means $x > y$ for $x > 0$. So the calibration curve must lie below the $45$-degree $y = x$ line, with $y = 0$ when $x = 0$.
Varying systematic error means the absolute error $x - y$ is not constant. It must increase with voltage, so the graph cannot be parallel to $y = x$ with a fixed offset.

A straight line through the origin with gradient less than 1, $y = k x$ with $k < 1$, gives $x - y = (1-k)x$, which grows in proportion to $x$. This matches larger readings and a voltage-dependent error.

At meter reading $4 \text{ V}$ the graph reaches only about $3.2 \text{ V}$ true, and at $2 \text{ V}$ it reaches about $1.6 \text{ V}$, so true is always smaller and the gap widens with voltage. This is option A.
